passage_text: Researchers at the University of Health Sciences conducted a study to examine how varying degrees of sleep deprivation affect cognitive performance in adolescents. One hundred fifty students aged 14–17 were recruited and randomly assigned to one of three sleep conditions: normal sleep (8 hours), moderate sleep deprivation (4 hours), and severe sleep deprivation (2 hours). After the assigned sleep period, each participant completed a computerized reaction time task designed to assess attention and processing speed. The mean reaction times (RT) and standard deviations (SD) for each group were recorded. The results indicated a clear dose–response relationship: adolescents who slept 8 hours had the fastest reaction times, while those who slept only 2 hours exhibited the slowest responses. These findings suggest that sleep deprivation significantly impairs cognitive function in this age group, with potential implications for academic performance and safety.
stem: Which sleep condition had the highest mean reaction time?

options.D: Moderate and severe sleep deprivation were equal

explanation: Correct: The severe (2 h) group had the highest mean RT (480 ms), the slowest responses. Why the others are wrong: A) Normal sleep had the lowest mean RT (350 ms). B) The 4 h group averaged 420 ms, below the 2 h group. D) Means were 420 and 480 ms, not equal.
trap: Picking the middle group, or confusing a higher RT with better performance.

stem: Which experimental design best supports a causal inference that sleep deprivation affects reaction time?

options.A: Cross‑sectional survey of adolescents’ sleep habits and test scores
options.B: Randomized controlled trial assigning participants to sleep conditions
options.C: Case‑control study comparing adolescents with and without sleep disorders
options.D: Longitudinal cohort study following adolescents over five years

explanation: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) randomly assigns participants to conditions, controlling for confounders and allowing causal inference. The other designs are observational and cannot definitively establish causality.
trap: Students may think a longitudinal cohort study provides causality because it follows participants over time, but without random assignment, confounding variables remain.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT a valid interpretation of the data?

options.A: Sleep deprivation leads to slower reaction times in adolescents.
options.B: The relationship between sleep loss and reaction time is dose‑dependent.
options.C: All adolescents in the severe sleep deprivation group performed worse than the normal sleep group.
options.D: Random assignment reduces the influence of confounding variables.

explanation: The data show group means, not individual performance. It is possible that some adolescents in the severe group performed better than some in the normal group.
trap: Students may assume that a higher mean automatically means every individual in that group performed worse.

stem: Which statement best links the study’s findings to real‑world implications for adolescents?

options.A: Insufficient sleep can slow attention and processing speed in adolescents, which matters for learning and safety.
options.B: Sleep deprivation has no measurable effect on cognitive tasks.
options.C: Only severe sleep loss affects adolescents, not moderate loss.
options.D: Reaction time is unrelated to school performance.

explanation: Correct: The 4 h and 2 h groups had slower mean reaction times (420 and 480 ms) than the 8 h group (350 ms), so insufficient sleep slowed a measure of attention and processing speed. Why the others are wrong: B) reaction times rose with sleep loss, so an effect was measured. C) the 4 h group was also slower than the 8 h group, so moderate loss had an effect. D) the study measured reaction time only and gives no evidence that reaction time is unrelated to school performance.
trap: Dismissing moderate sleep loss as harmless, overlooking the 70 ms slowdown in the 4 h group.
